titre: Peirce and the Four Ways of Believing
accroche: In 1877, an American logician sorts every way of ending doubt into four families, from the most comfortable to the most demanding.
contenu_vulgarise:
Doubt is uncomfortable, belief is a form of rest. Between the two, Charles Sanders Peirce writes in 1877 in “The Fixation of Belief,” published in the magazine Popular Science Monthly, he distinguishes four ways of fixing a belief, and only one of them relies on anything other than ourselves or society.

## Four methods

The first, the method of tenacity, consists in choosing a belief and sticking to it by avoiding anything that might contradict it. Peirce notes that it “is really pursued by many men,” and that it brings real peace of mind, as long as no one else interferes: it collapses on first contact with a neighbor who believes the opposite with the same confidence.

The second, the method of authority, hands belief over to an institution, religious or political, which imposes a doctrine and represses deviations. Peirce judges it more stable, since it erases contradiction by forbidding it: “let the will of the state act, then, instead of that of the individual.” It too fails once an individual notices that other societies, under other authorities, believe the opposite just as firmly.

The third, the a priori method, picks whatever seems reasonable, “agreeable to reason.” But what each person finds reasonable depends on their era and taste, not on experience: Peirce compares it to a fashion, one that changes from century to century without ever converging on a stable agreement.

What remains is the scientific method, which assumes that things have real characters, “entirely independent of our opinions about them,” and relies on experience to discover them. It is the only one of the four, Peirce writes, where any man, given enough experience and reasoning, will be led to the one true conclusion.

## What this shifts

The shift is not to say that science is right and the other three are wrong. Peirce grants each of the first three its own advantage: tenacity yields great peace of mind, authority governs the mass of mankind with proportionally far greater success, the a priori method offers comfortable conclusions. What sets the scientific method apart is that it is “the only one of the four methods” where one can go about it rightly or wrongly. With tenacity, whatever one thinks necessary to shut oneself off is necessary according to that method; with authority, the only test is what the state thinks, so it cannot pursue the method wrongly; with the a priori method, the point is to think as one is inclined to think. In the scientific method, by contrast, whether one is truly following the method is itself a matter of applying the method, not an immediate appeal to one's feelings and purposes. From this Peirce concludes that bad reasoning is possible as well as good, and that this fact is the foundation of the practical side of logic.

carte.punch: In 1877, a logician sorts every way of ending doubt into four families.
carte.idee: Charles Sanders Peirce distinguishes four methods for fixing belief in 1877: tenacity, authority, a priori reason, and the scientific method. Only the last distinguishes a right and a wrong way of going about it: the other three have no test beyond what one already thinks.

quiz.question: What sets the scientific method apart from the other three ways of fixing belief, according to Peirce?
choix: It is practiced by a majority of recognized scholars
It alone distinguishes a right and a wrong way of going about it
It alone brings real relief from doubt
It was imposed by an international scientific authority
quiz.explication: The first three methods also bring relief from doubt, and the scientific method owes nothing to any authority or to a number of practitioners. Peirce writes that it is the only one of the four where one can go about it rightly or wrongly: in the others, the test comes down to what one already thinks, what the state thinks, or what one is inclined to think.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why, according to Peirce, does the method of tenacity eventually collapse?
choix: Because an official authority eventually forbids it
Because it brings no real peace of mind
Because a neighbor believes the opposite with the same confidence
Because it requires too much accumulated experience
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Peirce writes that tenacity brings real peace of mind as long as no one else interferes; it collapses as soon as a neighbor believes the opposite with the same confidence.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Peirce, what makes the method of authority more stable than tenacity?
choix: It erases contradiction by forbidding it
It relies on experience and verifiable facts
It lets each individual judge for themselves
It changes from century to century, like fashion
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Peirce writes that the method of authority hands belief over to an institution that imposes a doctrine and represses deviations, which erases contradiction by forbidding it rather than resolving it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What, according to Peirce, characterizes the a priori method?
choix: It relies entirely on experience to settle questions
It imposes a single doctrine on the whole of society
It rests on what a majority of experts recognizes
It picks whatever seems reasonable, like a fashion that changes with the era
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Peirce compares the a priori method to a fashion: it picks whatever seems agreeable to reason, but that judgment depends on era and taste, and changes from century to century without converging.
